subject: ent
title: Complications of Otitis Media, Deep Abscesses, and Petrositis

steps.tx: Complications of otitis media arise when bacterial infection breaks out of the mucoperiosteal lining of the middle ear cleft to involve adjacent structures in the temporal bone or intracranial vault. Bone erosion occurs either via osteoclastic enzymatic lysis driven by cholesteatoma, or through retrograde progressive **thrombophlebitis** along small emissary venules bridging the intact bony tegmen and sinus plate.
steps.say: Otitis media complications occur via direct bone erosion from cholesteatoma or through retrograde thrombophlebitis traveling along emissary veins into the skull.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic showing pathways of intra- and extracranial complications of otitis media
vis.caption: Anatomical routes of otogenic infection spreading into deep neck spaces and intracranial fossae. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Complications are categorized into intratemporal (cranial) and intracranial complications. Intratemporal complications include acute mastoiditis, labyrinthitis, facial nerve palsy, petrositis, and subperiosteal abscesses. Intracranial complications represent life-threatening emergencies, encompassing extradural abscess, subdural empyema, meningitis, otitic brain abscess, and **lateral sinus thrombophlebitis**.
steps.say: Complications are split into intratemporal disorders like facial palsy and labyrinthitis, and life-threatening intracranial infections like brain abscess and sinus thrombosis.

steps.tx: When mastoid empyema perforates the cortex, pus follows distinct fascial and muscular planes to generate subperiosteal abscesses. Erosion of the outer cortex over MacEwen triangle forms a postauricular abscess. Perforation of the thin medial cortex of the mastoid tip forms a **Bezold abscess**, where pus tracks along the incisura mastoidea into the sheath of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, producing a deep brawny cervical neck mass.
steps.say: Eroding through the medial mastoid tip, pus tracks into the sternocleidomastoid sheath to form a deep cervical Bezold abscess with a brawny neck mass.

left.title: Bezold Abscess
points: Perforation through medial cortical wall of mastoid tip.
Presents as deep, tender, non-fluctuant upper neck mass.
May track down carotid sheath into superior mediastinum.

right.title: Luc Abscess
points: Pus tracks into deep posterosuperior bony canal wall.
Presents as sagging of posterosuperior meatus.
Extrudes directly into the external auditory meatus.

steps.tx: Other rare extracranial mastoid abscesses include the Citelli abscess and zygomatic abscess. A Citelli abscess arises when pus breaks through the digastric groove of the temporal bone to track along the posterior belly of the digastric muscle into the occipital and posterior cervical spaces. A **zygomatic abscess** develops in extensively pneumatized zygomatic roots, causing dramatic inflammatory swelling above and anterior to the ear with facial edema.
steps.say: A Citelli abscess tracks along the digastric muscle to the neck, while a zygomatic abscess expands forward over the zygomatic arch, causing facial and periorbital swelling.

vis.title: Subperiosteal Mastoid Abscess Topography
rows: Swelling above and in front of pinna

steps.tx: Petrositis refers to extension of infection into the pneumatized petrous apex of the temporal bone, occurring in approximately thirty percent of individuals who possess well-pneumatized apex cells. Petrositis manifests with the classic clinical triad of **Gradenigo syndrome**: persistent purulent otorrhea, deep retro-orbital or facial pain mediated by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), and ipsilateral abducens nerve palsy (CN VI).
steps.say: Gradenigo syndrome signals petrositis with three cardinal signs: ear discharge, retro-orbital trigeminal pain, and lateral rectus palsy from sixth nerve compression.

vis.alt: Anatomical diagram of temporal bone showing petrous apex, Dorello canal, abducens nerve, and trigeminal ganglion
vis.caption: Petrositis and Gradenigo syndrome: sixth nerve compression in Dorello canal and trigeminal involvement. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The sixth cranial nerve is uniquely vulnerable to petrous apex inflammation as it traverses Dorello canal beneath the petrosphenoidal ligament of Gruber. Compression here paralyzes the lateral rectus muscle, causing convergent strabismus and uncrossed horizontal **diplopia** maximal on gazing toward the side of the diseased ear. Meanwhile, edema of the adjacent Meckel cave inflames the trigeminal ganglion, generating excruciating ophthalmic facial pain.
steps.say: Passing through Dorello canal, the sixth cranial nerve is compressed by apical edema, causing horizontal double vision. Trigeminal irritation triggers intense retro-orbital pain.

nodes.label: Edema in Dorello Canal & Meckel Cave

steps.tx: Lateral sinus thrombophlebitis involves the sigmoid dural venous sinus secondary to an adjacent perisinus abscess. Contact of pus with the dura induces sinus wall necrosis and endophlebitis, seeding a mural thrombus that occludes the lumen. Shedding of septic emboli into the circulation causes the classic **picket-fence fever**, characterized by hectic daily temperature spikes with rigors followed by drenching diaphoresis.
steps.say: Sigmoid sinus thrombosis follows perisinus infection. Dislodged septic emboli trigger daily spiking picket-fence fevers accompanied by violent chills and drenching sweats.

vis.title: Clinical Progression of Lateral Sinus Thrombophlebitis
rows: Pus between sinus plate and dura

steps.tx: Management of lateral sinus thrombophlebitis combines emergency surgical intervention with medical therapy. The surgeon performs a complete cortical mastoidectomy, exposing the sinus plate, unroofing the dural sinus, and evacuating the perisinus abscess. Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and therapeutic **anticoagulation** with low-molecular-weight heparin are initiated to arrest propagation of the thrombus into the internal jugular vein.
steps.say: Treatment requires cortical mastoidectomy to decompress the sinus, intravenous antibiotics, and heparin anticoagulation to prevent thrombus extension into the jugular vein.
